claim: Phytophthora species cause diseases in a large variety of plants and represent a serious agricultural threat, leading, every year, to multibillion dollar losses.
source: Phytophthora species cause diseases in a large variety of plants and represent a serious agricultural threat, leading, every year, to multibillion dollar losses.
evidence: This is a general statement about Phytophthora's impact on agriculture, drawing from established scientific knowledge about plant pathogens.

claim: Infection occurs when biflagellated zoospores move across the soil at their characteristic high speed and reach the roots of a host plant.
source: Infection occurs when their biflagellated zoospores move across the soil at their characteristic high speed and reach the roots of a host plant.
evidence: This describes the infection mechanism of Phytophthora, based on established knowledge of the pathogen's life cycle.

claim: The mastigonemes-attached anterior flagellum is the main source of thrust in zoospores.
source: we show how these two flagella contribute to generate thrust when beating together, and identify the mastigonemes-attached anterior flagellum as the main source of thrust.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: During turning, the posterior flagellum temporarily stops while the anterior flagellum keeps beating.
source: we find that turning involves a complex active process, in which the posterior flagellum temporarily stops, while the anterior flagellum keeps on beating
evidence: This is directly observed in high-speed video recordings of zoospore turning events.

claim: The anterior flagellum changes its gait from sinusoidal waves to power and recovery strokes during turning.
source: the anterior flagellum keeps on beating and changes its gait from sinusoidal waves to power and recovery strokes, similar to Chlamydomonas's breaststroke, to reorient its body to a new direction.
evidence: This is observed in high-speed microscopy videos showing the flagellar beating patterns during turning events.

claim: The motility pattern of biflagellated zoospores represents a distinct eukaryotic version of the 'run-and-tumble' motility class exhibited by peritrichous bacteria.
source: Our study is a fundamental step toward a better understanding of the spreading of plant pathogens' motile forms, and shows that the motility pattern of these biflagellated zoospores represents a distinct eukaryotic version of the celebrated 'run-and-tumble' motility class exhibited by peritrichous bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed swimming patterns showing alternating straight runs and turning events, compared to bacterial motility.

claim: Escherichia coli possesses a bundle of passive helical flagella controlled by a rotary motor attached to the cell body.
source: Escherichia coli is one of the most studied prokaryotic swimmers, which possesses a bundle of passive helical flagella controlled by a rotary motor attached to the cell body (Turner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2000, indicating established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Eukaryotic microswimmers such as green algae Chlamydomonas and spermatozoa have active and flexible flagella along which molecular motors are distributed.
source: Eukaryotic microswimmers, such as green algae Chlamydomonas (Mitchell, 2001; Polin et al., 2009) and spermatozoa (Ishijima et al., 1986; Mortimer et al., 1997), have active and flexible flagella along which molecular motors are distributed.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the flagellar structure of eukaryotic swimmers.

claim: Phytophthora is classified as oomycetes and grouped in the kingdom of the Stramenopiles with the heterokont algae.
source: They are classified as oomycetes and grouped in the kingdom of the Stramenopiles with the heterokont algae (such as diatoms and brown algae) (Burki, 2014; Derelle et al., 2016).
evidence: This taxonomic classification is supported by citations to Burki, 2014 and Derelle et al., 2016.

claim: A number of Phytophthora species are plant pathogens and cause tremendous damages to agro- and eco-systems.
source: A number of Phytophthora species are plant pathogens and cause tremendous damages to agro- and eco-systems (Derevnina et al., 2016; Kamoun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Derevnina et al., 2016 and Kamoun et al., 2015.

claim: Phytophthora diseases are responsible for billions of dollars of damages each year and remain a threat to food security worldwide.
source: Nowadays, Phytophthora diseases are responsible for a big impact on economies with billions of dollars of damages each year and remain a threat to the food security worldwide (Drenth and Sendall, 2004; Judelson and Blanco, 2005; Strange and Scott, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple sources documenting the economic impact of Phytophthora diseases.

claim: Zoospore cell bodies store energy (mycolaminarin, lipid) allowing them to swim continuously for several hours.
source: To facilitate the spreading, their cell bodies store an amount of energy (mycolaminarin, lipid) allowing them to swim continuously for several hours (Judelson and Blanco, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Judelson and Blanco, 2005.

claim: P. parasitica is a polyphagous pathogen attacking a wide range of hosts including potato, onion, tomato, tobacco, ornamentals, cotton, pepper, citrus plants, and forest ecosystems.
source: In this study, we investigate the telluric species P. parasitica, a polyphagous pathogen attacking a wide range of hosts such as potato, onion, tomato, tobacco, ornamentals, cotton, pepper, citrus plants, and forest ecosystems (Panabieres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Panabieres et al., 2016.

claim: Potassium reduces zoospore swimming speed, causes immediate directional changes and results in perpetual circle trajectories.
source: For instance, potassium, which is uptaken by roots in the soil, reduces zoospore swimming speed, causes immediate directional changes and also results in perpetual circle trajectories (Appiah et al., 2005; Galiana et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Appiah et al., 2005 and Galiana et al., 2019.

claim: Potassium induces zoospore aggregation, which facilitates the advantages for zoospores to attack the host-root.
source: Bassani et al. provide transcriptomic studies showing that potassium induces zoospore aggregation, which facilitates the advantages for zoospores to attack the host-root (Bassani et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bassani et al., 2020b describing transcriptomic studies.

claim: Zoospore-zoospore interaction can lead to 'pattern swimming', a microbial bioconvection that happens without the appearance of chemical or electrical signals.
source: Experimental evidence has demonstrated that zoospore-zoospore interaction can lead to 'pattern swimming', a microbial bioconvection happened without the appearance of chemical or electrical signals (Ochiai et al., 2011; Savory et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ochiai et al., 2011 and Savory et al., 2014.

claim: A zoospore is usually about 10 µm in size and has a kidney-like cell body.
source: A zoospore is usually about 10 µm in size and has a kidney-like cell body (Mitchell et al., 2002; Walker and van West, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2002 and Walker and van West, 2007.

claim: The two flagella of zoospores beat longitudinally along the anterior-posterior axis of the cell body and not laterally as in the case of the green algae Chlamydomonas.
source: (i) The two flagella beat longitudinally along the anterior-posterior axis of the cell body and not laterally as in the case of the green algae Chlamydomonas;
evidence: This is an observation from the study comparing zoospore flagellar arrangement to Chlamydomonas.

claim: The anterior flagellum has a tinsel-like structure, while the posterior flagellum has a smooth whiplash structure.
source: (ii) two flagella distinguished from each other as the anterior flagellum has a tinsel-like structure, while the posterior flagellum has a smooth whiplash one, both beating periodically with wave propagation directions outwards the body.
evidence: This is observed through electron microscopy in the study.

claim: Multiple mastigoneme structures on the anterior flagellum of zoospores have thrust reversal ability.
source: Contrarily, multiple mastigoneme structures on the anterior flagellum of zoospores are shown to have thrust reversal ability, which makes both flagella generate thrust in the same direction and propel the cell body forwards (Bassani et al., 2020b; Cahill et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bassani et al., 2020b and Cahill et al., 1996.

claim: Mastigonemes are shown to generate thrust reversal in P. palmivora zoospores.
source: For instance, although mastigonemes are shown to generate thrust reversal in P. palmivora zoospores (Cahill et al., 1996), they do not contribute to enhance swimming of C. reinhardtii (Amador et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cahill et al., 1996.

claim: Mastigonemes do not contribute to enhance swimming of C. reinhardtii.
source: For instance, although mastigonemes are shown to generate thrust reversal in P. palmivora zoospores (Cahill et al., 1996), they do not contribute to enhance swimming of C. reinhardtii (Amador et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Amador et al., 2020.

claim: C. reinhardtii performs breaststroke swimming by two flagella drawing away and back to each other.
source: For examples, C. reinhardtii performs breaststroke swimming by two flagella drawing away and back to each other (Polin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Polin et al., 2009.

claim: E. coli and B. subtilis bacteria's flagella form a bundle and rotate together like a corkscrew to propel the cell body.
source: or E. coli, B. subtilis bacteria's flagella form a bundle and rotate together like a corkscrew to propel the cell body (Turner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2000.

claim: Carlile, 1983 describes that the anterior flagellum is responsible for pulling the zoospore through water whereas the posterior flagellum acts as a rudder for steering the cell.
source: Carlile, 1983 describes that the anterior flagellum is responsible for pulling the zoospore through water whereas the posterior flagellum acts as a rudder for steering the cell.
evidence: This is a claim from a cited source (Carlile, 1983).

claim: Morris et al., 1995 observe P. palmivora zoospores stop momentarily and then self-orientate their bodies to a new direction relatively to the posterior flagellum.
source: However, Morris et al., 1995 observe P. palmivora zoospores stop momentarily and then self-orientate their bodies to a new direction relatively to the posterior flagellum.
evidence: This is a claim from a cited source (Morris et al., 1995).

claim: Zoospores can perform long and stable straight runs, discontinued by active turning events.
source: We observe that zoospores can perform long and stable straight runs, discontinued by active turning events.
evidence: This is observed from trajectory analysis in the study.

claim: The cell body of P. parasitica has an ellipsoidal shape with tapered heads and a groove along the body.
source: The cell in general has an ellipsoidal shape with tapered heads and a groove along the body.
evidence: This is observed through Scanning Electron Microscopy.

claim: The posterior flagellum has a smooth whip shape with plenty of very fine hairs on the surface.
source: The posterior flagellum instead has a smooth whip shape with plenty of very fine hairs on the surface (Figure 1 (C3)).
evidence: This is observed through Transmission Electron Microscopy and shown in Figure 1(C3).

claim: Type-1 mastigonemes are tripartite hairs that occur in most of Stramenopiles kingdom and are known to be able to generate increased drag and reverse thrust for the anterior flagellum.
source: In contrary, the type-1 mastigonemes (Figure 1 (C5)) are tripartite hairs that occur in most of Stramenopiles kingdom. They are known to be able to generate increased drag and reverse thrust for the anterior flagellum (Cahill et al., 1996; Dodge, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cahill et al., 1996 and Dodge, 2012, and shown in Figure 1(C5).

claim: The cell body gyrates around the moving direction simultaneously during translation, resulting in a helical swimming trajectory.
source: While translating, the cell body gyrates around the moving direction simultaneously, which results in a helical swimming trajectory (see Video 4 for a long run of a zoospore swimming in water).
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings.

claim: The anterior flagellum can singly generate a speed threefold higher than the posterior flagellum can do at the same beating frequency.
source: For instance, the anterior flagellum can singly generate a speed threefold higher than the posterior flagellum can do at the same beating frequency.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model shown in Figure 3(E).

claim: At high frequencies, the anterior flagellum consumes approximately fivefold more power than the posterior, given the same beating frequency.
source: At high frequencies, the anterior flagellum consumes approximately fivefold more power than the posterior, given the same beating frequency.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model shown in Figure 3(F).

claim: When the frequency of the posterior flagellum is ~1.7-fold higher than that of the anterior flagellum, both flagella consume the same amount of power.
source: Interestingly, when the frequency of the posterior flagellum is ∼1.7-fold higher than that of the anterior flagellum, both flagella consume the same amount of power.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model shown in Figure 3(H).

claim: The propelling efficiency reaches its maximum value at ~1.2% when the beating frequency of the posterior is ~1.7-fold higher than that of the anterior flagellum.
source: The efficiency reaches its maximum value at ∼1.2 % when the beating frequency of the posterior is ∼1.7-fold higher than that of the anterior flagellum.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model shown in Figure 3(I).

claim: The anterior flagellum is the main motor of zoospores.
source: Taking the fact that the anterior flagellum can beat singly with the posterior flagellum staying on pause during turning events, we speculate that the anterior flagellum is the main motor of zoospores.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of flagellar behavior during turning and the modeling results.

claim: The turning event begins when the posterior flagellum instantaneously stops beating.
source: Then, the posterior flagellum instantaneously stops beating, which marks the beginning of a turning event (Figure 4 (A1-2)).
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: During turning, the zoospore performs two distinct sequences: rotation of the cell body and steering towards a new direction.
source: The zoospore then perform two distinct sequences of motions right after the posterior stops beating: (i) rotation of the cell body out of the old direction resulting from a few repetitive stroke-like beating of the anterior flagellum (Figure 4 (A3)), then (ii) steering towards a new direction as the anterior flagellum switches back to normal beating with sinusoidal waveform to propel the body (Figure 4 (A4-5)).
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The anterior flagellum performs continuous power and recovery strokes during the rotation step, similar to the breast-stroke beating of Chlamydomonas's flagella.
source: We observe that the anterior flagellum instantaneously perform continuous power and recovery strokes, similar to the breast-stroke beating of Chlamydomonas's flagella.
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings shown in Figure 4(E) and Video 6.

claim: The anterior flagellum beats at a higher frequency than usual (~110 Hz, compared to normally at ~70 Hz) during the stabilize step after turning.
source: We notice that in this step, the anterior flagellum beats at a higher frequency than usual (∼110 Hz, compared to normally at ∼70 Hz) and achieves a high-speed of ∼250 µm s-1.
evidence: This is measured from video analysis during turning events.

claim: The posterior flagellum does not act as a rudder to steer the direction.
source: Here, we can confirm that the posterior flagellum does not act as a rudder to steer the direction.
evidence: This is inferred from observations showing the posterior flagellum remains immobile during turning.

claim: The posterior flagellum might contribute to increase drag at one end of the cell body during turning.
source: Instead, it is fully stretched during turning events and might contribute to increase drag at one end of the cell body.
evidence: This is speculated based on observations of the posterior flagellum's position during turning.

claim: The posterior flagellum might contribute to chemical and electrical sensing.
source: The function of the posterior flagellum is not completely clear regarding thrust production during translation or turning. Thus, we speculate that it might contribute to other non-physical activities such as chemical and electrical sensing.
evidence: This is speculated based on the unclear function of the posterior flagellum in thrust production.

claim: The motility pattern of zoospores represents an Eukaryotic version of the 'run-and-tumble' motility class exhibited by peritrichous bacteria.
source: It is worth stressing the motility pattern exhibited by the zoospores represents an Eukaryotic version of the 'run-and-tumble' motility class exhibited by bacteria peritrichous bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed swimming patterns showing alternating straight runs and turning events.

claim: C. reinhardtii has been reported to fall into the run-and-tumble motility category.
source: Several eukaryotic swimmers, for example spermatozoa, do not exhibit such kind of motility pattern, but C. reinhardtii have been reported to also fall into this category (Polin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Polin et al., 2009.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, reorientation events occur during asynchronous beating periods of the two identical flagella, while straight runs require synchronous beating.
source: Reorientation events occur during asynchronous beating periods of the two identical flagella, while straight runs require synchronous beating.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Chlamydomonas motility.

claim: In zoospores, straight runs involve coordinated beating of the opposite and different flagella, while turning involves temporary halting of posterior flagellum.
source: In sharp contrast to this picture, we show that in zoospores while straight runs also involve a coordinated beating of the opposite and different flagella, turning involves temporary halting of posterior flagellum, while the anterior flagellum continues beating.
evidence: This is observed from high-speed video analysis of zoospore swimming.

claim: P. parasitica navigates using a fundamentally different internal regulation mechanism to control swimming than C. reinhardtii.
source: This strongly suggests that P. parasitica navigates using a fundamentally different internal regulation mechanism to control swimming, than C. reinhardtii, a mechanism that is likely to be present in other Eukaryotic swimmers with two opposite and different flagella.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in flagellar coordination between zoospores and Chlamydomonas.

claim: The anterior flagellum contributes more to zoospore speed although energy is shared in comparable manner between both flagella.
source: We show that although the energy is shared in comparable manner between both flagella, the anterior flagellum contributes more to zoospore speed.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical modeling and experimental observations.

claim: Zoospores actively change directions thanks to the sole beating of the anterior flagellum.
source: Zoospores actively change directions thanks to the sole beating of the anterior flagellum.
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings of turning events.

claim: The anterior flagellum is in charge of generating speed and changing beating patterns from sinusoidal wave to power and recover stroke to quickly rotate the body.
source: We believe that anterior flagellum could be the main motor of zoospores that is in charge of generating speed, changing beating patterns from sinusoidal wave to power and recover stroke to quickly rotate the body
evidence: This is inferred from observations and modeling of flagellar behavior during swimming and turning.

claim: The posterior flagellum might play a role in chemical/electrical sensing and providing an anchor-like turning point for zoospores.
source: while the posterior flagellum might play a role in chemical/electrical sensing and providing an anchor-like turning point for zoospores, instead of acting like a rudder as previously hypothesized.
evidence: This is speculated based on observations of the posterior flagellum's behavior during turning.

claim: P. parasitica mycelium is cultured routinely on malt agar at 24°C in the dark.
source: We culture mycelium of Phytophthora parasitica (isolate 310, Phytophthora INRAE collection, Sophia-Antipolis, France) (Bassani et al., 2020b; Galiana et al., 2019) routinely on malt agar at 24 °C in the dark.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Zoospores are released from sporangia by a heat shock procedure involving refrigeration at 4°C for 30 min followed by pouring 37°C distilled water and incubation at room temperature for 30 min.
source: Zoospores are released from sporangia by a heat shock procedure. We place a petri-dish of mycelium inside a refrigerator at 4 °C for 30 min, then pour 10 mL of 37 °C distilled water on top of the mycelium and continue to incubate it at room temperature (25 °C) for another 30 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The appearance of mastigonemes results in a reversed thrust from the anterior flagellum.
source: The plot shows that the appearance of mastigonemes results in a reversed thrust from the anterior flagellum.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 3(D).

claim: When changing directions, zoospores swim with the solely beating anterior flagellum to pull the body forwards while the posterior flagellum is immobile.
source: Interestingly, when changing directions, zoospores are observed to swim with the solely beating anterior flagellum to pull the body forwards while the posterior flagellum is immobile (Figure 4(A)) and Video 5, which confirms the thrust reversal ability of the mastigonemes.
evidence: This is observed in high-speed video recordings shown in Figure 4(A) and Video 5.

claim: The front flagellum of zoospores has fibrillar mastigonemes at higher density with tubular shape and larger in size than Chlamydomonas.
source: The front flagellum of zoospores has fibrillar mastigonemes, similar to Chlamydomonas, but at higher density with tubular shape and larger in size, that could render into account of the different beating properties from the smooth posterior flagellum.
evidence: This is observed through electron microscopy and compared to Chlamydomonas.

claim: High mastigoneme density (more than 20 per 1 μm flagellum length) shows mild effect on speed.
source: However, high mastigoneme density (more than 20 per 1 µm flagellum length) shows mild effect on speed.
evidence: This is shown by the mathematical model in Figure 3(D).

claim: Zoospores achieve a high-speed of ~250 μm/s during the stabilize step after turning.
source: We notice that in this step, the anterior flagellum beats at a higher frequency than usual (∼110 Hz, compared to normally at ∼70 Hz) and achieves a high-speed of ∼250 µm s-1.
evidence: This is measured from video analysis during turning events.

claim: The gyrational motion of the cell body might result from the intrinsic chiral shape of the zoospore body and off-axis arrangement of their flagella.
source: We believe that this gyrational motion might result from the intrinsic chiral shape of the zoospore body and off-axis arrangement of their flagella (Figure 1(B)).
evidence: This is speculated based on observations and comparison to previous studies on chiral microswimmers.

claim: Previous studies have shown that chirality of a microswimmer's body induces spontaneous axial rotation resulting from the translational motion.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that chirality of a microswimmer's body induces spontaneous axial rotation resulting from the translational motion (Keaveny and Shelley, 2009; Löwen, 2016; Namdeo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Keaveny and Shelley, 2009; Löwen, 2016; Namdeo et al., 2014.

claim: Each flagellum of zoospores beats as a flexible oar in a 2D plane.
source: The observations of helical trajectories also confirm that each flagellum of zoospores beat as a flexible oar in a 2D plane as we notice the two flagella flattened into two straight lines during the gyration.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of helical trajectories.

claim: Zoospores are not expected to swim in circles when interacting with no-slip boundaries as seen in case of E. coli with a rotating flagellar bundle.
source: Thus, zoospores are not expected to swim in circles when interacting with no-slip boundaries as seen in case of E. coli with a rotating flagellar bundle.
evidence: This is inferred from the 2D planar beating of flagella and compared to E. coli behavior.

claim: The 'curved straight runs' of zoospores observed in trajectories might result from rotational diffusion and thermal fluctuations.
source: The 'curved straight runs' of zoospores that we observed in Figure 2(A) might result from rotational diffusion and thermal fluctuations.
evidence: This is speculated based on observations in Figure 2(A).

claim: Resistive Force Theory has proven to be an effective and accurate method to predict the propulsive force and velocity of microswimmers regardless of the interactions of flagellum-flagellum or flagellum-body.
source: RFT has proven to be an effective and accurate method to predict the propulsive force and velocity of microswimmers regardless of the interactions of flagellum-flagellum or flagellum-body (Gray and Hancock, 1955; Lauga and Powers, 2009; Marcos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray and Hancock, 1955; Lauga and Powers, 2009; Marcos et al., 2014.

claim: Hydrodynamic interactions between neighboring mastigonemes can be neglected due to their rigidity.
source: As a result, hydrodynamic interactions between neighboring mastigonemes can also be neglected.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculated rigidity of mastigonemes.

claim: The effects of the type-2 mastigonemes in producing drag are ignored due to their non-tubular and random structures.
source: Additionally, we ignore the effects of the type-2 mastigonemes in producing drag due to their non-tubular and random structures.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on observations of type-2 mastigoneme structure.

claim: The turning mechanism of zoospores allows them to actively and quickly achieve a new direction, which is not the case of other microswimmers such as the tumbling of E. coli or Chlamydomonas.
source: The advantage of zoospore turning mechanism is that it allows them to actively and quickly achieve a new direction, which is not the case of other microswimmers such as the tumbling of E. coli's (Darnton et al., 2007; Perez Ipiña et al., 2019) or Chlamydomonas's (Bennett and Golestanian, 2015; Polin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from observations of zoospore turning and compared to other microswimmers with citations.
